_note: Eleven v3 narration, one entry per video section (S1-S11, matching docs/NARRATION.md and docs/CODEX-RECORDING-PROMPT.md). Written to be spoken: short sentences, contractions, ellipses and [pause]/[short pause] tags for natural breaks. Square-bracket tags are v3 audio tags and are not spoken. No brand drug names; never the word 'safe'.

sections.name: hook
sections.text: [conversational] So... Sarah takes fluoxetine. It's an antidepressant. [short pause] And today, her doctor wants to give her codeine, for pain. [pause] Her DNA test? Says she processes painkillers... normally. [short pause] So, the prescription looks fine. [pause] [serious] It's not.

sections.name: sarah
sections.text: [thoughtful] Here's the thing. Your liver has this, like, cleanup crew for medicines... and your DNA decides how fast that crew works. [short pause] But some drugs jam the crew. [short pause] Fluoxetine's one of them. [pause] So Sarah's genes still say normal... [short pause] but right now? Her body's slow. [confident] And RxGene catches that. Codeine probably won't relieve her pain, so... her doctor should avoid it, and pick something else.

sections.name: same-genes
sections.text: [matter-of-fact] Same genes. [short pause] Different response. [pause] Her gene report, on its own, says normal. And a regular interaction warning? It's the same for everybody. [short pause] RxGene puts the two together... and tells you what's actually true for Sarah, today.

sections.name: evidence
sections.text: [calm] And every alert shows its work. [short pause] The guideline it comes from, how strong the evidence is, the score before and after... and the exact numbered rules behind it. [pause] The FDA reports down here? Those are just context. [short pause] Never proof.

sections.name: marcus
sections.text: [calm] Now, Marcus. [short pause] He was already slow, just from his genes. So he still gets the codeine warning... [short pause] but RxGene tells you straight up: the fluoxetine doesn't change anything for him. [short pause] One clear alert. Not two noisy ones.

sections.name: lena-tom
sections.text: [curious] It works the other way too. [short pause] When Lena's doctor adds fluoxetine, RxGene goes back and re-checks the codeine she's already on. [pause] [serious] And if a gene result can't be read, like Tom's here... it just says so. Ask a pharmacist. [short pause] No guessing.

sections.name: agent
sections.text: [engaged] For pharmacists, there's an AI agent that reviews the whole medication list. [short pause] It calls our rule engine for every single drug... then drafts a consult note, and every sentence points back to the step it came from. [pause] [serious] But the AI never decides an alert. [short pause] If even one citation doesn't check out... it falls back to a plain template.

sections.name: patient
sections.text: [warm] And patients get a plain-language version. [short pause] In English... or in Spanish.

sections.name: ehr
sections.text: [confident] It also plugs right into hospital systems. [short pause] RxGene is a real CDS Hooks service, that's the standard for decision support inside health records. [short pause] So here, a public test EHR is calling it... while a doctor orders codeine.

sections.name: kiro
sections.text: [proud] We built all of this with Kiro, spec first. [short pause] Our genetics teammate wrote over fifty clinical rules before there was any code... and Kiro checked them for conflicts. [short pause] [excited] Then Kiro's property-based tests caught two engine bugs our examples completely missed. [pause] [confident] And Kiro hooks stop the coding agent from touching the clinical data it's tested against.

sections.name: close
sections.text: [warm] Your genes don't change. [pause] Your prescriptions do. [short pause] [confident] This is RxGene.
